chapter: Cafe Society and the Zodiac Suite
title: Deering's Farm, the jam with Ellington's band, and Orlando Wright
summary: Leading her own band at Deering's Farm, with singer Joe Williams, she hosted Duke Ellington's men. Orlando Wright astonished Ben Webster by playing 'Body and Soul' in all keys, and Art Blakey learned time.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: ...Deering's Farm and we had a very successful run there. We went in in August and stayed there till October or September. Everything was going great. We had on our bill a great blues singer, Joe Williams who I thought was fabulous. I had never heard anyone sing like him before - and a stage show there. Everything was going fine until Duke Ellington's band came to town and they happened to hear about us being there. Ben Webster and all the cats including Duke Ellington came out to the farm... I had such fabulous musicians. I didn't know how great they were until the night that Duke Ellington and these guys came in there. They had played an engagement in Cleveland. We did our show and we had a jam session and I think Baby Lee Laurence the great tap dancer was with them, so we really

had a ball that night. Ben Webster took out his horn, he came up and jammed with us and I discovered that Orlando Wright whose name is now Musa Kalim was just about one of the greatest tenor men going. He was around 17 or 18 years old. So Ben got up on the stand and he was blowing "Body and Soul" so when it came time for Orlando to take his solo he said, he stuttered, "Miss-miss-miss Williams, E natural." I said, "Oh, my goodness." He played it in E natural and before he finished he said, "B natural." He played in all these keys and Ben Webster looked at him with his big eyes and said, "Well, man, that's too much for me!" Art Blakey's time wasn't too good. Hal and I used to have to sit on the stand with him with his foot marking time, but he was really blowing. He could swing like mad. We trained him, the both of us. We were just almost in between him, like the piano was here and Art Blakey was there and Hal Baker was next to him. So at the end of about 2 or 3 weeks he was really good. His time didn't vary, it wasn't noticeable rather. But what happened, when I went home that night I discovered - no, it was the next morning when I woke up - I got ahead of myself. Hal Baker and I had married, you know. We got married before he left the band, before they came through Pittsburgh on their way to another city. I discovered that Hal was nowhere around the next morning when I got up.
